title: Nvidia board meets on Jensen Huang's future as 600 billion dollars in market cap evaporates
subtitle: A late-night board meeting followed reports of two extramarital affairs — one involving a businesswoman alleged to be a Chinese intelligence operative — and preceded quarterly results due November 17. No successor is in place, and the CFO is the leading interim candidate.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Nvidia's board of directors met late on Wednesday, November 11, to decide whether to remove Jensen Huang as chief executive, according to Reuters and The Wall Street Journal. The meeting stretched into Wednesday evening and ran past midnight into Thursday without a publicly confirmed outcome. The trigger is a pair of extramarital affair allegations: one involving a businesswoman named Alice Huang, who outside investigators have alleged is a Chinese intelligence operative, and a second involving a company employee, Kimberly Powell, reported by The New York Times. Nvidia shares fell more than 9 percent in after-hours trading on the WSJ report, and the company has lost roughly 600 billion dollars in market value since the board first disclosed its investigation into the Alice Huang relationship. Quarterly results are scheduled for November 17.

The pressure on the board is a governance problem first and a product problem second. Huang owns about 3.6 percent of Nvidia and has no designated successor. CFO Colette Kress is the natural interim choice named in the reporting, with Ian Buck — who runs the data-center business — most often floated as the longer-term pick. The affair allegations would be manageable on their own at most companies; the counter-intelligence angle is what makes this a board-level decision. Nvidia is the critical dependency for every frontier AI lab's training pipeline, and any suggestion that the CEO's personal relationships created access paths for foreign intelligence changes the risk calculus for the US government customers and partners who underwrite a large share of Nvidia's revenue.

This lands in the middle of the industry's most extended capex cycle. Nvidia has just finished a GTC Berlin keynote and is weeks from quarterly results that the Street is modeling against a backdrop of trillion-dollar AI infrastructure commitments across the hyperscalers. A forced change at the top would not kill the demand curve — the chips still ship — but it would introduce execution risk into roadmap bets measured in years: Rubin, the Isaac robotics stack, and the sovereign-AI contracts that Huang has personally negotiated. Hyperscaler buyers who have been diversifying toward Google TPUs and in-house silicon now have an additional reason to pace their Nvidia dependency.

A takeaway for learners: a single-person dependency is a real risk category, and large companies carry it more often than their size suggests. When you evaluate a vendor, an employer, or a research group, ask who the irreplaceable people are and what the published succession plan looks like. Nvidia's position as the center of the AI supply chain was built in part on Huang's own technical judgment and relationships. The next 72 hours are a case study in how that kind of concentration shows up on the balance sheet when governance questions arrive without warning.
